title: Auto-retries pushed task success to 94% — did retries fix reliability?

scenario.role: You're the data engineer on platform reliability at Orbit
scenario.situation: Last quarter the platform bumped default task retries from 1 to 3 across every DAG. Nadia, the platform lead, pulled task-run logs from before and after the change: overall task success climbed from 92.1% to 94.0%. She's ready to present retries as the reliability win of the quarter and make 3 retries the permanent standard. She wants you to confirm the numbers before the all-hands.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: "Bumping retries to 3 lifted task success ~2 points across the board. Retries fixed our reliability — let's make it the standard."
scenario.question: Did the retry change actually improve reliability? Confirm what really moved between the two periods, and tell Nadia whether retries deserve the credit.

columns.name: dag_id
columns.description: Which DAG the task belongs to

columns.name: task_class
columns.description: Kind of task: sensor (cheap polling), transform, load, or ml

columns.name: period
columns.description: before or after the retry change

columns.name: max_retries
columns.description: Configured retries for the run: 1 before, 3 after

columns.name: succeeded
columns.description: 1 if the task ultimately succeeded, else 0 — the outcome

guidingQuestions: Reproduce Nadia's number: overall task success rate in the before period vs the after period.
Now compute success rate by task_class WITHIN each period. What happens to each class — sensor, transform, load, ml — from before to after?
Compare the mix of task classes across the two periods. What share of tasks are cheap sensor tasks before vs after?
If every class got worse but the overall rate went up, what must be true about how the task mix changed — and which metric is telling the truth about reliability?
Retries went 1 → 3 in the same window. Given the per-class picture, do retries deserve the credit for the headline — and what actually happened to the work that matters?
suggestedApproach: Reproduce the aggregate first: overall success by period.
Never trust an aggregate across a changing mix — break success down by task_class within each period before concluding anything.
If the subgroup story disagrees with the aggregate, look at the mix: compute each class's share of tasks per period.
Decide which number answers the reliability question — the blended rate over a shifted mix, or the like-for-like within-class rates.
Separate the two things that happened at once (retry bump + a monitoring-driven sensor flood) and say what each did, rather than crediting the retry change for a mix artifact.

notebook.intro: Five steps: reproduce the reliability number, break it down by task class, and decide which number answers the question.

cells.title: Reproduce the aggregate
cells.explain: Overall success rate before and after — the number in the claim.
cells.code:
overall = df.groupby("period")["succeeded"].mean() * 100
raw_change = overall["after"] - overall["before"]
print(f"change: {raw_change:+.2f} pts")
overall.round(2)
cells.reads: Success really is higher after. The question is whether the same work is being measured.

cells.title: Break it down by task class
cells.explain: Never trust an aggregate across a changing mix. Compare success within each task_class in each period.
cells.code:
by_class = df.groupby(["task_class", "period"])["succeeded"].mean().unstack() * 100
by_class["change"] = by_class["after"] - by_class["before"]
by_class.round(2)
cells.reads: Read the change column class by class and compare it with the aggregate change from cell 1.

cells.title: Look at the mix
cells.explain: If the classes disagree with the aggregate, look at what share of tasks each class contributes per period.
cells.code:
share = pd.crosstab(df["period"], df["task_class"], normalize="index") * 100
print("share of tasks by class, per period (%)")
share.round(1)
cells.reads: One class's share moves sharply between the periods — that is the monitoring rollout, not a reliability change.

cells.title: Hold the task mix constant
cells.explain: Re-weight both periods to one common class mix so the composition cannot move the number.
cells.code:
within = df.groupby(["task_class", "period"])["succeeded"].mean().unstack()
weights = df["task_class"].value_counts(normalize=True)
adjusted = within.mul(weights, axis=0).sum() * 100
held_change = adjusted["after"] - adjusted["before"]
print(f"mix-adjusted change: {held_change:+.2f} pts")
adjusted.round(2)
cells.reads: Like-for-like, the improvement is a different size from the headline.

cells.title: Separate the two events
cells.explain: The retry bump and the sensor flood landed together. Split the headline into the part retries could explain and the part the mix explains.
cells.code:
pd.DataFrame(
    {"pts": [raw_change, held_change, raw_change - held_change]},
    index=["aggregate change", "within-class (retries)", "from task mix (sensors)"],
).round(2)
cells.reads: Crediting the retry change with the whole headline would credit it for a change in what was being run.

teachingNote.naiveRead: Overall task success rose from 92.1% before to 94.0% after the retry bump — about +1.9 points. Taken at face value, moving to 3 retries improved reliability and should be the new standard.
teachingNote.theTrap: The aggregate reversed on a mix shift — Simpson's paradox. The retry rollout coincided with a monitoring push that flooded the schedulers with cheap sensor tasks (near-100% success): sensors went from 30% of all tasks before to 75% after. Because the mix tilted hard toward the highest-success class, the blended rate rose even though EVERY class got worse: sensor 99.3% → 96.9%, transform 90.2% → 85.9%, load 89.5% → 85.2%, ml 85.8% → 83.4%. A concurrent dependency upgrade quietly regressed real execution, and retries didn't fix it. The headline is measuring the task mix, not reliability.
teachingNote.honestAnswer: Reliability got WORSE, not better. Within every task class success fell by 2-4 points in the after period; the +1.9 point aggregate is an illusion created by the surge of trivially-successful sensor tasks diluting the pool. Retries deserve no credit — if anything they masked a real regression on transform/load/ml, the work that actually matters. Tell Nadia not to present retries as a win: report the per-class rates, investigate what regressed the pipeline tasks (the dependency upgrade in the same window), and track success on a fixed task mix (or weight by class) so a change in what runs can't masquerade as a change in how well it runs.
howToGetThere: Reproduce the aggregate: mean(succeeded) by period → 92.1% before, 94.0% after (+1.9 pts).
Break it down: mean(succeeded) by task_class within period → every class is LOWER after (sensor 99.3→96.9, transform 90.2→85.9, load 89.5→85.2, ml 85.8→83.4).
Explain the reversal via mix: share of sensor tasks is 30% before vs 75% after — the pool tilted toward the highest-success class.
Reconcile: a size-weighted or fixed-mix success rate (hold class shares constant) shows a decline, matching the per-class story.
Attribute correctly: the retry bump and a sensor flood happened together; the aggregate rise is the mix, and the within-class fall is the real signal.

numbers.label: Sensor share of tasks — before vs after

teachingNote.lesson: An aggregate rate over a changing population can move opposite to every subgroup inside it — Simpson's paradox. Here a flood of easy sensor tasks lifted the blended success rate while the actual work regressed underneath it. Whenever a headline metric spans a mix that shifted, disaggregate before you attribute the change to anything: compute the rate within stable subgroups, and check whether the group shares moved. Two things happened at once (more retries, more sensors); the reflex is to separate them, not to credit the intervention you were hoping worked. Track reliability on a fixed or weighted task mix so composition changes can't fake a win.
